prompt: What makes a bird's bones light enough for flight?
exp_tip: A drinking straw is hard to bend for its weight. A bird's bone works the same way.

prompt: Which part of a bird's chest anchors its flight muscles?
exp_tip: Same word as the keel of a boat, and the same shape: a blade standing on edge.

prompt: Why does air flowing over a wing lift the bird?
exp_tip: Hold a flat hand out of a moving car and tilt it. That push is lift.

prompt: What is the small tuft of feathers on the leading edge of a wing called?
exp_tip: Watch a pigeon land: a small feather flicks up at the front of each wing.

prompt: What is a bird's wishbone made from?
exp_tip: Its other name says what it does: the furcula, from the Latin for little fork.

prompt: How does air travel through a bird's lungs?
exp_tip: Yours is a bellows going in and out; a bird's is a loop that only ever goes round.

prompt: Which bird can fly backwards?
exp_tip: Its wingtip draws a figure of eight in the air rather than an arc.

prompt: Which wing shape suits a bird that must turn sharply among trees?
exp_tip: Look at where a bird lives, and you can guess the shape of its wing.

prompt: How does an albatross cross an ocean with almost no flapping?
exp_tip: It is not gliding down but zig-zagging between two speeds of wind.

prompt: Why do many large birds fly in a V?
exp_tip: The bird in front works hardest, so the flock keeps swapping it.

prompt: What are feathers made of?
exp_tip: A feather is dead tissue. That is why moulting exists at all.

prompt: How does a duck keep its feathers from soaking through?
exp_tip: Wash a duck with soap and it sinks. The feathers are fine; the oil is gone.

prompt: Why does a blue jay's feather look blue?
exp_tip: Red survives being crushed. Blue does not. The difference is pigment against structure.

prompt: What gives a flamingo its pink colour?
exp_tip: Chicks hatch grey. The pink takes two or three years to arrive.

prompt: What holds the flat surface of a flight feather together?
exp_tip: Split a feather down the middle, then stroke it. It knits itself shut.

prompt: What is moulting?
exp_tip: Matching pairs, left and right together, so the bird stays balanced in the air.

prompt: What is down used for?
exp_tip: A duvet works the same way, and for the same reason it is useless once wet.

prompt: Why are many female birds duller than the males?
exp_tip: The plumage follows the job, not the sex. Phalaropes prove it by reversing both.

prompt: Roughly how many feathers does a swan carry?
exp_tip: The count follows the cold, not the bird's size.

prompt: How does a bird use its feathers to keep warm on a freezing morning?
exp_tip: The rounder the robin, the colder the morning.

prompt: What is a bird's beak made of?
exp_tip: It keeps growing and keeps wearing. Stop the wear and it grows out of shape.

prompt: What do birds use instead of teeth to grind their food?
exp_tip: The grit a chicken picks up is not an accident. It is the bird collecting its teeth.

prompt: What is a crossbill's crossed beak for?
exp_tip: Some cross to the left, some to the right, and each works its own side of the cone.

prompt: How does a flamingo feed?
exp_tip: The beak looks deformed until you turn the bird's head over.

prompt: Why does hammering wood not injure a woodpecker?
exp_tip: The tongue is anchored above the eye and wraps the skull. It is padding as much as a tongue.

prompt: What is a pelican's throat pouch for?
exp_tip: The pouch holds around three times what the stomach can. It is a net, not a larder.

prompt: Which beak shape belongs to a seed eater?
exp_tip: Look at any beak and ask whether it is built for reach or for force. It is never both.

prompt: What is a toucan's enormous beak mainly good for?
exp_tip: At night the toucan tucks the beak under a wing — the radiator, switched off.

prompt: How does a hummingbird get nectar out of a flower?
exp_tip: For a hundred years this was taught as capillary action. Slow-motion film disproved it.

prompt: Why does a heron stand still for so long in shallow water?
exp_tip: Water bends light, so a fish is never quite where it looks. The heron allows for it.

prompt: Why are the eggs of cliff-nesting birds so sharply pointed at one end?
exp_tip: Look at the egg and you can guess the nest. Pointed means no walls.

prompt: What is an egg shell made of?
exp_tip: An egg breathes. Seal the pores with varnish and the chick suffocates.

prompt: What is an egg tooth?
exp_tip: The chick breathes air trapped inside the shell before it ever reaches the outside.

prompt: Which living bird lays the largest egg?
exp_tip: Biggest in absolute terms, smallest in relative terms. The kiwi holds the opposite record.

prompt: What does a cuckoo do instead of raising its own young?
exp_tip: The chick evicts its nestmates within hours of hatching, before its eyes have opened.

prompt: Why are the eggs of ground-nesting birds usually speckled?
exp_tip: Hole-nesters lay white. Open-ground nesters lay speckled. The nest predicts the egg.

prompt: What is a clutch?
exp_tip: Eggs make a clutch. Once they hatch, the same family is called a brood.

prompt: How do megapodes keep their eggs warm without sitting on them?
exp_tip: The chick hatches able to fly, and is never fed by an adult. Not once.

prompt: Why does a sitting bird turn its eggs several times a day?
exp_tip: Every incubator ever built has a turning motor. This is the only reason it is there.

prompt: Which bird weaves the most elaborate hanging nest?
exp_tip: If the female refuses the nest, the male dismantles it and rebuilds from scratch.

prompt: Which bird travels the longest distance each year?
exp_tip: It lives in almost perpetual summer, and sees more daylight than any creature on Earth.

prompt: Why do birds migrate?
exp_tip: Insect-eaters leave, seed-eaters stay. Sort any garden by diet and the pattern appears.

prompt: What do migrating birds burn as fuel?
exp_tip: The gut shrinks before departure and regrows on arrival. The body is rebuilt for the trip.

prompt: Which bird holds the record for the longest flight without landing?
exp_tip: It sleeps one brain hemisphere at a time, with the matching eye shut.

prompt: How does a night-migrating bird find its direction?
exp_tip: Shown a false sky in a planetarium, a bird turns to match it. That settled the argument.

prompt: How does a young bird find its way the first time it migrates alone?
exp_tip: Move a young bird sideways and it misses. Move an adult and it corrects. Experience makes the map.

prompt: What is a stopover site?
exp_tip: A flyway is only as strong as its scarcest stopover. Lose one and the chain breaks.

prompt: Which bird crosses the Himalayas at heights where a climber can barely move?
exp_tip: They climb through valleys rather than over peaks, taking the thickest air available.

prompt: Why do many small birds migrate at night?
exp_tip: Weather radar picks them up. On peak nights the display fills with birds, not rain.

prompt: What tells a bird that the time to leave has come?
exp_tip: Caged migrants flutter towards their route at the right season. The urge does not need the journey.

prompt: Which organ does a bird sing with?
exp_tip: The name means the same as a set of pan pipes. It has two sides for good reason.

prompt: How can some birds sing two different notes at the same time?
exp_tip: A wood thrush harmonises with itself. There is no second bird.

prompt: What is the difference between a bird's song and its call?
exp_tip: Alarm calls are pitched to be hard to locate. The warning carries; the caller does not.

prompt: Are birds born knowing their song?
exp_tip: Young birds babble before they sing properly. The stage is called subsong.

prompt: Which bird is the most accomplished mimic?
exp_tip: Mimicked sounds pass from male to male and can outlast whatever made them.

prompt: Why do birds sing most intensely at dawn?
exp_tip: The chorus has an order, and it holds night after night. Big eyes start earliest.

prompt: Which bird makes the loudest call yet recorded?
exp_tip: He saves the loudest call for a female at arm's length, and turns to aim it at her.

prompt: What is a dialect in birdsong?
exp_tip: Copying plus isolation is all it takes. The same recipe that gives human accents.

prompt: In Europe, which birds usually do the singing?
exp_tip: Tropical pairs duet so tightly that two birds sound like one. The female half is easy to miss.

prompt: How do birds in noisy cities make themselves heard?
exp_tip: During lockdown, city birds dropped their pitch again within weeks. The adjustment is live.

prompt: Which is the largest bird alive?
exp_tip: Its eye is about 5 cm across — bigger than its brain.

prompt: What is missing from the chest of a flightless bird?
exp_tip: Penguins have no flight and a huge keel. They still fly — in water.

prompt: How does a penguin move underwater?
exp_tip: Its bones are solid, not hollow. Every other bird's are the opposite.

prompt: Why did so many island birds lose the ability to fly?
exp_tip: Rails have lost flight independently on dozens of islands. The same answer, over and over.

prompt: What was the dodo's closest relative?
exp_tip: Its ground nests, not its meat, were what the rats and pigs destroyed.

prompt: Which flightless bird is considered the most dangerous?
exp_tip: Its boom is close to the lower limit of human hearing. You feel it before you hear it.

prompt: What is unusual about a kiwi's nostrils?
exp_tip: Loose hair-like feathers, whiskers, burrows, a low body temperature. Almost a mammal.

prompt: How fast can an ostrich run?
exp_tip: Two toes, not four. The inner one has become almost a hoof.

prompt: Which is the smallest flightless bird?
exp_tip: It survives because nobody could land there. That is the entire conservation story.

prompt: What does a kakapo do that no other parrot does?
exp_tip: They breed only when the rimu trees fruit — some years apart. That is the bottleneck.

prompt: What does light travel through space as?
exp_tip: Two slits give waves. One metal plate gives particles. Both experiments are real.

prompt: Does light need something to travel through?
exp_tip: In space nobody hears an explosion, but everybody sees it.

prompt: What is a photon?
exp_tip: A dark-adapted human eye can register a handful of photons. Possibly one.

prompt: What makes one colour of light different from another?
exp_tip: Three kinds of cone, and every colour you know is a ratio between them.

prompt: Why can you see a wooden table but not the air in front of it?
exp_tip: A red apple is red because it absorbs everything else and rejects red.

prompt: What happens to the light that a black surface receives?
exp_tip: Coat a crumpled shape in the blackest material and it looks like a flat hole.

prompt: What happens to light when it enters water?
exp_tip: The bend happens only at the surface. Inside the water the light runs straight again.

prompt: Why does a mirror send back such a clear picture?
exp_tip: A wet road reflects; a dry one does not. The water has filled the roughness.

prompt: Where does the light of the Sun come from?
exp_tip: The light warming your face left the core before humans existed. The last eight minutes were the quick part.

prompt: Why does a lamp filament glow when it gets hot enough?
exp_tip: You are glowing right now, in infrared. A thermal camera sees you in your own light.

prompt: How fast does light travel through empty space?
exp_tip: The metre is defined from this speed, so the number can never change again.

prompt: How long does sunlight take to reach the Earth?
exp_tip: Gravity travels at the same speed as light. Both messages arrive together.

prompt: What is a light-year?
exp_tip: Read any distance in light-years twice: once as far, once as long ago.

prompt: Which star is nearest to the Sun?
exp_tip: Our fastest probe would take six thousand years. Light takes four.

prompt: What happens to light's speed when it passes through glass?
exp_tip: The speed limit is for a vacuum. Inside matter, light always lags.

prompt: Why can nothing with mass reach the speed of light?
exp_tip: A photon cannot slow down or speed up. It has one speed, and no other.

prompt: How long does moonlight take to reach the Earth?
exp_tip: Mirrors left on the Moon still return laser pulses. The timing gives the distance.

prompt: Why does thunder arrive after the lightning that caused it?
exp_tip: Seconds between flash and bang, divided by three: the distance in kilometres.

prompt: When you look at a distant galaxy, what are you seeing?
exp_tip: Want to see the past? Look further away. There is no other method.

prompt: How was the speed of light first shown to be finite?
exp_tip: Galileo had tried with lanterns on two hills. Light crossed the gap far too fast to catch.

prompt: What does a glass prism do to a beam of white light?
exp_tip: Two prisms in a row give white again. The glass sorts; it does not colour.

prompt: Why do the colours separate as light passes through glass?
exp_tip: The order never changes: red bends least, violet most, always in that sequence.

prompt: Which colour of visible light has the shortest wave?
exp_tip: The whole of human colour vision fits inside one doubling of wavelength.

prompt: Why does a lemon look yellow?
exp_tip: Under a pure red lamp a lemon looks red-black. It has no yellow left to give back.

prompt: What do you get when you mix red, green and blue light?
exp_tip: Look at a white screen through a magnifier. There is no white lamp, only three coloured ones.

prompt: Why does a soap bubble show shifting bands of colour?
exp_tip: A bubble turns black at the top just before it pops. That is the film at its thinnest.

prompt: What is a spectrum?
exp_tip: Helium was discovered in sunlight, twenty-seven years before anyone found it here.

prompt: Why does a rainbow always show its colours in the same order?
exp_tip: The second bow of a double rainbow runs backwards. Two bounces instead of one.

prompt: Why can a bee see patterns on a flower that you cannot?
exp_tip: Bees see barely any red. To them, a red poppy reads as dark.

prompt: Why does the sea look blue-green as you go deeper?
exp_tip: At 20 metres a red wetsuit looks black. Shine a torch on it and the red returns.

prompt: Where must the Sun be for you to see a rainbow?
exp_tip: Your shadow points at the bow's centre. The rainbow is a circle drawn around your head.

prompt: What happens to sunlight inside a single raindrop?
exp_tip: Not one bend but two, with a bounce between them. That is where the colour comes from.

prompt: Which colour lies on the outer edge of a rainbow?
exp_tip: The entire band is about two degrees wide — four Moons, side by side.

prompt: Why does the second bow of a double rainbow show its colours reversed?
exp_tip: The sky between the two bows is darker than outside them. No drop sends light there.

prompt: Can two people standing side by side see the same rainbow?
exp_tip: You can never reach the end of one, because there is no end and no object to reach.

prompt: What shape is a rainbow really?
exp_tip: From a plane you see the whole ring, with the aircraft's shadow dead centre.

prompt: Why is a fogbow almost white instead of coloured?
exp_tip: Big drops make a sharp bow, small drops a broad white one. The size sets the sharpness.

prompt: Why does a garden hose make a rainbow on a sunny day?
exp_tip: Spray with the Sun behind you and step sideways. The bow moves with you, precisely.

prompt: Can a rainbow appear at night?
exp_tip: Your eye sees it grey. A long photographic exposure shows every colour.

prompt: Why do the colours of a rainbow blend rather than form seven clean bands?
exp_tip: Indigo was added to make seven, to match the notes of a scale. Nothing in the light asked for it.

prompt: Why is the daytime sky blue?
exp_tip: Above the atmosphere the sky is black, even with the Sun blazing. No air, no scattering.

prompt: Why does the sky turn red at sunset?
exp_tip: Sunset red is what is left over, not something new. The blue went elsewhere.

prompt: Why is the sky black when seen from space?
exp_tip: On the Moon it is daylight and night sky at once. Bright ground, black sky, hard shadows.

prompt: Why do distant mountains look pale blue?
exp_tip: Painters call it aerial perspective. The furthest ridge is always the palest.

prompt: Why do clouds look white rather than blue?
exp_tip: White and grey clouds are made of the same thing. Grey ones are simply deeper.

prompt: Why is the Sun's disc yellow at midday but orange near the horizon?
exp_tip: After a large volcanic eruption, sunsets around the world stay red for months.

prompt: Why does the Sun look flattened as it touches the horizon?
exp_tip: When the Sun appears to touch the horizon, it is already below it. You are seeing a bent image.

prompt: What is the green flash sometimes seen at sunset?
exp_tip: Blue is bent even further but never survives the trip. Green is the highest colour that arrives.

prompt: Why does the sky glow after the Sun has gone down?
exp_tip: In a polar summer the Sun never gets 18 degrees down. Twilight simply never ends.

prompt: Why is the setting Sun safe to look at when the midday Sun is not?
exp_tip: During a partial eclipse the Sun looks dim and is not. That is what makes eclipses dangerous.

prompt: What lies just beyond the red end of visible light?
exp_tip: It was found by a thermometer placed where there was nothing to measure.

prompt: What does a warm body give off that the eye cannot detect?
exp_tip: A thermal camera needs no light source. You are the source.

prompt: What lies just beyond the violet end of visible light?
exp_tip: A window blocks most ultraviolet. You do not tan behind glass.

prompt: Why does ultraviolet light burn skin when brighter red light does not?
exp_tip: Turning a red lamp up cannot burn you. A dim ultraviolet lamp can.

prompt: How does a bee benefit from seeing ultraviolet?
exp_tip: Some birds we cannot tell apart are obviously different to one another in ultraviolet.

prompt: What do radio waves and visible light have in common?
exp_tip: The visible part is a sliver. The full range spans a factor of a million billion.

prompt: Why can X-rays show the bones inside a hand?
exp_tip: The first X-ray image was a hand with a wedding ring, made in 1895.

prompt: How can a telescope show a cloud of gas that is completely dark to the eye?
exp_tip: Those black patches across the Milky Way are not empty. They are opaque.

prompt: Which invisible light reaches us from the earliest universe?
exp_tip: Old analogue television static held a trace of it. A fraction of that noise was the early universe.

prompt: Why do humans see only such a narrow band of all this light?
exp_tip: The atmosphere has two clear windows: visible light, and radio. We use both.

prompt: What is a shadow?
exp_tip: A shadow's edge can outrun light itself, because nothing is actually moving along it.

prompt: Why does a shadow have blurred edges in daylight?
exp_tip: Your feet cast a sharp shadow, your head a soft one. Same Sun, different distance.

prompt: Why is your shadow longest early and late in the day?
exp_tip: When your shadow is exactly your own height, the Sun sits 45 degrees up.

prompt: Why do you have two overlapping shadows under two lamps?
exp_tip: Count a footballer's shadows under floodlights. The number tells you how many lamps there are.

prompt: What does a solar eclipse consist of?
exp_tip: The Sun is 400 times wider and 400 times further. That coincidence is what makes totality possible.

prompt: Why do the shadows of leaves make round spots of light on the ground?
exp_tip: During a partial eclipse, every spot under a tree becomes a crescent. All at the same moment.

prompt: Why is a shadow on Earth never completely black?
exp_tip: Shadows look bluish because it is the blue sky doing the lighting.

prompt: What must be true for an object to cast no shadow at all?
exp_tip: A white object casts as dark a shadow as a black one. Colour changes nothing.

prompt: Why does a lunar eclipse turn the Moon red rather than black?
exp_tip: Standing on the Moon during one, you would see Earth as a black disc ringed in red fire.

prompt: How can a shadow be used to tell the time?
exp_tip: The rod is tilted to your latitude. That is what keeps the hours evenly spaced all year.

prompt: What causes day and night?
exp_tip: Sitting still at the equator, you are moving east at over 1,600 km/h.

prompt: Which way does the Earth turn?
exp_tip: On Venus the Sun rises in the west. It is one of the few worlds spinning the other way.

prompt: How long does the Earth take to turn once relative to the stars?
exp_tip: Stars rise four minutes earlier each night. Over a year that is one full circuit.

prompt: Why is it not the same time everywhere on Earth at once?
exp_tip: Every town kept its own noon until the railways. Timetables ended that.

prompt: Where does the Sun stay above the horizon for months at a time?
exp_tip: Everywhere gets the same annual daylight. Only the delivery schedule differs.

prompt: Why is the sky dark at night if there are billions of stars?
exp_tip: The dark sky is itself a clue. An eternal, infinite universe would glare.

prompt: Why do the stars appear to wheel around one point in the sky?
exp_tip: Polaris sits as high above the horizon as your latitude. Measure it and you know where you are.

prompt: Why does the Moon show the same face to us at all times?
exp_tip: Far side, not dark side. It has days and nights like anywhere else.

prompt: What is happening when the Moon is visible in the daytime sky?
exp_tip: Only the full Moon is truly a night object. It rises exactly as the Sun goes down.

prompt: Why does a day on Earth grow very slightly longer over time?
exp_tip: Fossil corals show years of 400 days. The days were shorter then, so more of them fitted.

prompt: Why does day length change through the year?
exp_tip: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter.

prompt: What happens at the summer solstice?
exp_tip: Solstice is Latin for the Sun standing still. For days it stops climbing before turning back.

prompt: What is an equinox?
exp_tip: On an equinox the Sun rises due east everywhere on Earth. It is the one day compasses agree.

prompt: Why is the hottest weather several weeks after the longest day?
exp_tip: Same reason the hottest part of a day is mid-afternoon rather than midday.

prompt: How does day length vary at the equator through the year?
exp_tip: Equatorial twilight lasts minutes. The Sun drops straight down rather than sliding along.

prompt: Why is summer warmer than winter?
exp_tip: A torch aimed straight down makes a small bright spot. Tilt it and the same light spreads thin.

prompt: Why does the Sun rise at a different point on the horizon through the year?
exp_tip: Stonehenge marks the solstice sunrise. It is a calendar made of the horizon itself.

prompt: What happens at the poles at the equinox?
exp_tip: A pole gets one sunrise a year, and it takes about two days to finish.

prompt: Why does the earliest sunset not fall on the shortest day?
exp_tip: Earliest sunset comes before the solstice, latest sunrise after. The shortest day sits between.

prompt: What would happen to the seasons if the Earth's axis were upright?
exp_tip: Uranus is tipped 98 degrees. Each of its poles gets 42 years of daylight in a row.

prompt: What is twilight?
exp_tip: Twilight is sunlight arriving by a detour, bounced down from air you cannot see.

prompt: How far below the horizon must the Sun be for full darkness?
exp_tip: The nautical stage is named for the window when both horizon and stars can be seen at once.

prompt: Why does twilight last so long in northern countries in summer?
exp_tip: Above 60 degrees in June the Sun never gets 18 degrees down. Night never properly starts.

prompt: Why is the sky often pink opposite the setting Sun?
exp_tip: The dark strip below the pink is the Earth's shadow. You are watching it climb.

prompt: What are crepuscular rays?
exp_tip: The beams look to spread from a point. They are parallel. It is only perspective.

prompt: Why do colours fade as evening comes on?
exp_tip: Red flowers go black at dusk while blue ones stay visible. Your rods prefer blue.

prompt: How long does the eye take to reach full sensitivity in the dark?
exp_tip: Red light barely disturbs dark adaptation. That is why bridges and observatories use it.

prompt: Why do many animals become active at dawn and dusk?
exp_tip: The word is crepuscular. Deer, rabbits and most cats live by it.

prompt: Why does the dawn chorus of birds happen when it does?
exp_tip: The order of the chorus follows eye size. Big-eyed birds start first.

prompt: Why can you sometimes see satellites shortly after sunset?
exp_tip: Watch one long enough and it fades out mid-sky. It has entered the Earth's shadow.

prompt: What is darkness?
exp_tip: You cannot shine darkness at a wall. There is nothing to shine.

prompt: Where on Earth can a person experience total darkness?
exp_tip: The eye invents images when starved of input. Cave explorers see flashes that are not there.

prompt: Why is a moonless country night never truly black?
exp_tip: Airglow means the atmosphere itself shines faintly, every night, everywhere.

prompt: How deep does sunlight reach into the ocean?
exp_tip: Most of Earth's habitable volume is permanently dark. The lit part is a thin skin.

prompt: How do creatures of the deep sea find one another in the dark?
exp_tip: Almost all of it is blue, because blue travels furthest through water.

prompt: What happens to an animal's eyes over generations in permanent darkness?
exp_tip: The Mexican tetra exists in both forms, sighted and blind, and they can still interbreed.

prompt: Why is the inside of a black hole described as dark?
exp_tip: The first image of one showed a black disc ringed by brilliant light. The ring is matter falling in.

prompt: Why can a shadow never be perfectly dark in open air?
exp_tip: On the Moon a shadow really is black. Apollo crews could not see into their own.

prompt: How much light can a fully dark-adapted eye detect?
exp_tip: A single rod cell fires on one photon. The eye is near the limit physics allows.

prompt: Why do fewer stars appear over a large town?
exp_tip: Under a truly dark sky the Milky Way is bright enough to cast a shadow.

prompt: Why do many night animals have very large eyes?
exp_tip: An owl's eyes cannot move. It rotates its head because it has no other choice.

prompt: What are the rod cells of the eye for?
exp_tip: To see a faint star, look slightly beside it. The centre of your retina has no rods.

prompt: Why do a cat's eyes shine when a light catches them at night?
exp_tip: Red-eye in photographs is blood, not a mirror. We have no tapetum at all.

prompt: How does an owl catch a mouse it cannot see?
exp_tip: Its ears are at different heights on purpose. That is what gives it up-and-down aim.

prompt: How does a bat find an insect in complete darkness?
exp_tip: Some moths hear the bat coming and jam its sonar with clicks. The arms race is live.

prompt: What does a pit viper's heat-sensing organ detect?
exp_tip: The heat signal reaches the visual part of the brain. The snake effectively sees warmth.

prompt: Why does a cat's pupil open so wide at night?
exp_tip: A goat's pupil stays horizontal even when it lowers its head. The eye rotates to keep it level.

prompt: Why can a moth find a mate on a night with no light at all?
exp_tip: It took the scent glands of half a million moths to isolate the first known pheromone.

prompt: Why do so many night-active animals have poor colour vision?
exp_tip: Some geckos see colour by starlight — where a human sees nothing but grey.

prompt: How can a dung beetle steer a straight line on a moonless night?
exp_tip: Researchers fitted beetles with small hats to blind them. Only then did they wander.

prompt: What is the mirror behind a night animal's retina called?
exp_tip: The name means bright carpet. It is laid behind the retina, not over it.

prompt: What does an animal give up by having a tapetum?
exp_tip: Eagles have no tapetum. They hunt by day and spend everything on sharpness.

prompt: Why do human eyes come out red in a photograph?
exp_tip: Move the flash away from the lens and red-eye disappears. The angle is the whole cause.

prompt: Why does eyeshine differ in colour between species?
exp_tip: Sweep a torch over a swamp and every pair of red points is a crocodile.

prompt: How can a spider be found at night with a headtorch?
exp_tip: The torch must be level with your eyes. Held to one side, the points vanish.

prompt: Why does a cat's eye seem to glow when the room is not fully dark?
exp_tip: In a sealed cave a cat's eyes show nothing. There is nothing to give back.

prompt: Why do a cat's pupils narrow to slits rather than small circles?
exp_tip: Lions have round pupils, house cats have slits. Size of the hunter decides it.

prompt: Why do grazing animals such as goats have horizontal pupils?
exp_tip: Watch a goat lower its head. The eyes roll to keep the slits horizontal.

prompt: Which animal has the largest eyes of any on Earth?
exp_tip: The eye is that big for one purpose: spotting the glow a sperm whale disturbs as it swims.

prompt: Why does an owl turn its whole head instead of moving its eyes?
exp_tip: Its neck arteries have deliberate slack, so twisting 270 degrees does not throttle the blood supply.

prompt: How does an animal work out which direction a sound came from?
exp_tip: Ten millionths of a second between ears is enough for your brain to place a sound.

prompt: Why is a barn owl's face shaped like a shallow dish?
exp_tip: It can change the shape of its face to focus. The disc is adjustable.

prompt: What makes an owl's flight almost silent?
exp_tip: The silence is as much for the owl's own hearing as for the mouse's ignorance.

prompt: How does a bat avoid deafening itself with its own calls?
exp_tip: The muscle fires just before each call and relaxes for the echo, two hundred times a second.

prompt: How does a dog find a trail hours after it was made?
exp_tip: A dog can tell which way a trail runs, by comparing the strength between two footprints.

prompt: Why does a snake flick its tongue in and out?
exp_tip: The fork exists so the two tips can be compared. Smell with a left and a right.

prompt: How do whiskers help an animal move in the dark?
exp_tip: A seal can follow the trail a fish left in the water half a minute before, by whisker alone.

prompt: How does a mole find its way underground?
exp_tip: The star-nosed mole can smell underwater, by exhaling bubbles and re-inhaling them.

prompt: How does a shark detect a fish hidden under sand?
exp_tip: A hidden fish cannot switch off its heartbeat. That is the signal the shark reads.

prompt: Why can an elephant communicate with another many kilometres away?
exp_tip: Some of it travels through the ground. Elephants listen through their feet.

prompt: How does a dolphin sleep without drowning?
exp_tip: Ducks at the edge of a group sleep with the outward eye open. Those in the middle do not.

prompt: How does a swift sleep during months in the air?
exp_tip: A young swift may not land at all until it is two years old and ready to nest.

prompt: Why can a horse sleep standing up?
exp_tip: For deep sleep it must lie down. Herds take turns, and one stays standing.

prompt: What is hibernation?
exp_tip: Hibernators must warm up periodically to sleep properly. Hibernation is not restful.

prompt: Does a bear truly hibernate?
exp_tip: It emerges having lost fat but almost no muscle. Nobody has worked out how to copy that.

prompt: How long does a giraffe sleep each day?
exp_tip: Sleep tracks safety. Lions sleep twenty hours; the animals they hunt sleep barely one.

prompt: Why do bats hang upside down to rest?
exp_tip: A bat cannot take off from the ground. Hanging up high is how it launches.

prompt: How does a sea otter avoid drifting away while it sleeps?
exp_tip: Rafts of sleeping otters hold paws. It keeps the group from scattering overnight.

prompt: What is unusual about the way birds sleep during migration?
exp_tip: Frigatebirds sleep 40 minutes a day in flight and over 12 hours a day on land.

prompt: Why do nocturnal animals sleep through the day?
exp_tip: In permanent darkness the rhythm continues, drifting slightly. Daylight only resets it.

prompt: Why are night-blooming flowers usually white?
exp_tip: Under moonlight, a red flower reads as black. A white one glows.

prompt: Why do night flowers give off such a strong scent?
exp_tip: Many of them switch the scent on and off by the clock. It costs too much to run all day.

prompt: Which insect pollinates most night-opening flowers?
exp_tip: The flower's tube length and the moth's tongue length match closely. Neither works without the other.

prompt: What did Darwin predict from the shape of a Madagascan orchid?
exp_tip: The moth was named praedicta — the predicted one. Nobody filmed it feeding until 1992.

prompt: How does a flower know when to open?
exp_tip: Linnaeus designed a garden bed you could read the time from. Each species opened at its own hour.

prompt: What is unusual about the flowering of the night-blooming cereus?
exp_tip: Whole populations bloom on the same night. Synchrony is what makes one night enough.

prompt: Why do some tropical flowers open at night for bats?
exp_tip: Some flowers have petals shaped to bounce a bat's sonar back at it. A reflector, not a colour.

prompt: Why do many flowers close their petals at night?
exp_tip: A tulip opens and closes by uneven growth. Bring one indoors and it stays open for good.

prompt: How does a moth locate a flower from far away in the dark?
exp_tip: The zig-zag is not confusion. Each turn is a deliberate search for the lost plume.

prompt: Why does a moonflower open in a matter of minutes?
exp_tip: Every plant movement there is comes from water shifting between cells. There is no muscle anywhere.

prompt: What is bioluminescence?
exp_tip: It has been invented independently over forty times. Nature keeps arriving at the same answer.

prompt: Why is bioluminescence called cold light?
exp_tip: About 90% of the energy becomes light. Hold a firefly and you feel nothing.

prompt: What two ingredients does most bioluminescence need?
exp_tip: Many animals control the glow by controlling oxygen. Cut the supply and the light goes out.

prompt: Where does most of the world's bioluminescence occur?
exp_tip: Bioluminescence is almost unknown in fresh water, and nobody has fully explained why.

prompt: Why is nearly all ocean bioluminescence blue?
exp_tip: Some dragonfish shine red, a colour their prey cannot see. A searchlight nobody else can detect.

prompt: How does an anglerfish use its light?
exp_tip: The fish does not make the light. Bacteria do, and it houses and feeds them for it.

prompt: How does glowing on its underside help a deep-sea fish hide?
exp_tip: Some species measure the light above and adjust their own glow to match. In real time.

prompt: Why do some sea creatures release a cloud of light when attacked?
exp_tip: Some prey glow to attract a bigger predator to eat the one chasing them. A burglar alarm.

prompt: What is the commonest use of light among fireflies?
exp_tip: Some females imitate another species' reply, then eat the male who answers. They are called femmes fatales.

prompt: Why does the glow of many bacteria only start when there are enough of them?
exp_tip: The bobtail squid ejects most of its bacteria every morning and lets them regrow by night.

prompt: What kind of animal is a firefly?
exp_tip: Firefly, glow-worm, lightning bug — three names, one beetle, and none of them accurate.

prompt: How does a firefly switch its light on and off so sharply?
exp_tip: The signal is a nerve telling nearby cells to stop using oxygen. The light gets what they release.

prompt: What does a female firefly's answering flash tell the male?
exp_tip: In a meadow with six species flashing at once, the timing is what keeps them apart.

prompt: How does a Photuris female trap males of other species?
exp_tip: She eats them partly to steal a defensive chemical she cannot make, then puts it in her eggs.

prompt: What is a glow-worm, in most cases?
exp_tip: The larvae hunt snails many times their size, and take days to finish one.

prompt: What is remarkable about the fireflies of some Southeast Asian rivers?
exp_tip: Nobody leads. Each one nudges its rhythm towards its neighbours, and order appears on its own.

prompt: What do New Zealand cave glow-worms use their light for?
exp_tip: The hungrier the larva, the brighter it shines. Hunger sets the wattage.

prompt: Why do firefly eggs and larvae glow as well?
exp_tip: Larvae glow even in species whose adults do not. The warning is older than the courtship.

prompt: Why are fireflies becoming harder to find in many places?
exp_tip: Switching lights off during the season measurably brings them back. The fix is that direct.

prompt: Where on a firefly's body is the light produced?
exp_tip: The scales over the lantern were copied to make LEDs brighter. The beetle got there first.

prompt: At roughly what depth does the deep sea begin?
exp_tip: Ninety per cent of the ocean's volume is below the sunlit layer.

prompt: How many deep-sea animals produce their own light?
exp_tip: In coastal water, roughly one species in forty glows. In the deep, three quarters of the groups do.

prompt: Why is nearly all deep-sea light blue?
exp_tip: A few species break the rule. Tomopteris glows yellow, which nobody has fully explained.

prompt: What advantage does a dragonfish gain by shining red?
exp_tip: Many deep-sea animals are red precisely because red is invisible down there. The dragonfish defeats that.

prompt: What is counter-illumination?
exp_tip: Sensors on the body read the light above and set the belly to match. Automatically.

prompt: Where does an anglerfish's light actually come from?
exp_tip: The bobtail squid vents most of its bacteria at dawn and lets the colony rebuild by nightfall.

prompt: Which is the most abundant fish of the deep sea?
exp_tip: Sonar showed a seabed that rose every night. It was fish, and there were that many of them.

prompt: Why do deep-sea animals still have working eyes if no sunlight reaches them?
exp_tip: Cave animals go blind, deep-sea animals do not. The difference tells you the deep sea is not dark.

prompt: What do many deep-sea animals do every night?
exp_tip: It happens every day, everywhere, and by mass it dwarfs every migration on land.

prompt: What are milky seas?
exp_tip: Satellites have photographed one. No research ship has ever managed to reach a large one in time.

prompt: What is the glow of certain fungi in a wood at night called?
exp_tip: Fox here likely comes from an old word for false. A false fire, cold and harmless.

prompt: What part of a glowing fungus produces the light?
exp_tip: Pick up a glowing log and you are holding the fungus, not the wood.

prompt: Roughly how many species of fungi are known to glow?
exp_tip: Finding new ones requires standing in a dark forest with the light switched off. Nobody does that by accident.

prompt: Which mushroom is famous for its bright green glow?
exp_tip: Chanterelles grow from soil, jack-o'-lanterns from wood. That difference has saved a lot of dinners.

prompt: What colour is the light of glowing fungi?
exp_tip: You need a good twenty minutes in the dark before your eyes can pick most of them out.

prompt: What is the leading explanation for why fungi glow?
exp_tip: Fake mushrooms with a light inside caught far more insects than identical dark ones.

prompt: Why does glowing wood give off no heat?
exp_tip: Coal miners are said to have carried it as a lamp. A flame down there could kill everyone.

prompt: What does a glowing fungus feed on?
exp_tip: Very little on Earth can digest wood. Without these fungi, dead trees would simply accumulate.

prompt: How is it possible to make a plant glow using fungal genes?
exp_tip: Firefly genes needed a fuel plants lack. Fungal genes needed one plants already had.

prompt: Why is a glowing fungus so hard to notice on an ordinary walk?
exp_tip: One look at a phone screen undoes half an hour of dark adaptation.

prompt: What makes a wave glow blue as it breaks at night?
exp_tip: Footprints on wet sand glow for a second or two. Each step crushes millions of them.

prompt: What sets off the flash of a glowing plankton cell?
exp_tip: The flash follows the touch in about twenty milliseconds. It is drawing what moved.

prompt: Why would a single-celled drifter flash when disturbed?
exp_tip: It is sometimes called the burglar alarm hypothesis. You cannot escape, so you make noise.

prompt: What is a red tide?
exp_tip: The same bloom can be an ugly brown stain by day and the most beautiful thing you have seen by night.

prompt: What is a bioluminescent bay?
exp_tip: Several bays that once glowed have gone permanently dark after building work near the shore.

prompt: How did glowing plankton once betray ships at sea?
exp_tip: A dolphin swimming through a bloom is outlined in light, exactly like its own shape.

prompt: Are glowing plankton animals or plants?
exp_tip: The name means whirling whip. They spin as they swim, driven by two tails at right angles.

prompt: Why do glowing plankton flash mostly at night?
exp_tip: A single cell with no brain keeps a 24-hour clock, and keeps it in permanent darkness.

prompt: Where is the light produced inside one of these cells?
exp_tip: The trigger is a sudden change of acidity inside the sac. That is what fires the flash.

prompt: What is the best way to see glowing plankton?
exp_tip: Stir the water yourself. The plankton only flash when something disturbs them — so you make the show.
